headline: Take-Two gets hammered -5.7% on GTA VI leak chaos while US-Iran tensions spike oil prices and rattle global markets — a mixed day for the portfolio overall.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO had a rough night last session, tumbling 5.7% after news broke that Take-Two's investigation into the GTA VI leaker has hit a new intensity — described as 'rapidly evolving'. Markets are spooked that the ongoing leak saga could delay or complicate the GTA VI release, which is the single biggest catalyst the stock is betting on. For a long-term holder this is noise unless the game itself is delayed, but it's a stock to watch closely.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google fell 2.2% last session, weighed down by reports of a YouTube revenue delay adding to investor concerns about rising AI spending eating into profits. Despite earnings rising 24% in Q2, the market is nervous about how much Alphabet is spending on AI infrastructure. The underlying business remains strong — this looks more like sector jitters than a structural problem.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft slipped 1.2% last session, caught in the same broad tech sell-off that hit the NASDAQ. Nothing company-specific drove the move — analysts continue to flag Microsoft as a top AI infrastructure play, with one report noting its AI investment dwarfs Tesla's. The long-term data centre buildout story is intact.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI bounced nicely today, up 2.1% on the ASX, tracking positive sentiment around AI as a structural growth theme. The ETF's exposure to global AI names is still seen as a long-term growth play, even as individual tech stocks remain volatile.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS gained 1.5% today — a welcome green day, though the lithium market remains challenged overall. A strike vote at Chilean miner Albemarle is adding some supply-side uncertainty globally, which may have given lithium stocks a small lift. The path to a sustainable recovery for PLS depends on lithium prices finding a floor — still a watch-and-wait situation.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE edged up 0.24% today — a quiet session for emerging markets. No major catalyst; the ETF continues to track broadly with global risk sentiment.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG nudged up 0.2% today, doing what it does — quietly compounding. No specific catalyst; the diversified nature of this ETF means it absorbs daily volatility smoothly. Exactly what you want from a core holding.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS dipped just 0.16% today, reflecting last night's mild NASDAQ and S&P 500 falls flowing through the ASX-listed ETF. Essentially flat — nothing to worry about here for a long-term holder.

watch_today.title: TTWO: GTA VI Leak Investigation Escalating
watch_today.detail: Take-Two dropped 5.7% last night on news that the GTA VI leak investigation is 'rapidly evolving' — the company says they nearly tracked down the leaker. This is a real risk: if the investigation causes internal disruption or forces a game delay, the investment thesis (GTA VI as a blockbuster revenue event) takes a hit. For now the game isn't confirmed as delayed, so the long-term case still holds — but this is worth watching closely this week.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Down -2.2% on YouTube Revenue Concerns
watch_today.detail: Google fell on reports of a YouTube revenue delay and rising AI spending concerns, despite posting 24% earnings growth in Q2 2026. The underlying business is genuinely strong — cloud revenue surged and the stock has been hovering near $339 recently. A single-session dip on spending fears isn't a reason to exit a quality compounder. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: PLS: Small Green Day — But Don't Get Too Excited Yet
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals gained 1.5% today, helped partly by supply uncertainty from a strike vote at Chilean lithium giant Albemarle. PLS is still down 18.7% overall in your portfolio. The lithium price recovery needs to be more sustained before this turns the corner. Keep holding — the long-term electrification story is intact, but patience is required.

watch_today.title: Oil Spiking — Watch for Inflation Knock-On
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) jumped 2.45% last night to $87.86/barrel after US and Iran exchanged fire in a new flare-up. Sustained high oil prices feed through to fuel, transport and goods costs — potentially giving the RBA more reason to keep interest rates higher for longer. Worth watching as a macro risk for Australian consumers and the broader market.

watch_today.title: GXAI: AI ETF Recovering — Long-Term Thesis Intact
watch_today.detail: GXAI gained 2.1% today on the ASX, and the broader AI investment theme continues to attract attention globally, with the US pushing 'light-touch' AI regulation at the G20. You're still down 11.1% on this position overall, but AI as a structural growth theme isn't going away. Hold and give it time.

watch_today.title: RBA Rate Hike Risk Building — Watch Your Mortgage
watch_today.detail: Multiple analysts are warning that Australians haven't got the RBA's message on cutting spending, and rate hikes could still be on the table. Both the RBA and the US Fed are being described as 'hawkish' (meaning they're leaning toward raising rates, not cutting them). This is relevant to anyone with a variable-rate mortgage and also affects growth stocks in your portfolio.

world.summary: The dominant global story today is a renewed US-Iran military confrontation, which has sent oil prices surging and left airlines scrambling. Meanwhile, Trump is pushing for minimal AI regulation at the G20 and continuing his domestic political purge.

stories.title: US and Iran Exchange Fire in Major New Flare-Up
stories.why_it_matters: After a period of relative quiet, the US and Iran have exchanged direct military strikes, ending what many were calling a 'lull' in their conflict. President Trump has threatened to hit Iran 'hard' with further action. This is a significant escalation — direct US-Iran military exchanges risk drawing in regional powers and disrupting Middle East stability. For everyday Australians, the most immediate impact is at the petrol pump: oil jumped 2.45% overnight on supply fears, and if the conflict deepens, fuel prices could rise further.

stories.title: Oil Surges 2.5% as US-Iran Conflict Stokes Supply Fears
stories.why_it_matters: Crude oil (WTI) jumped from $85.76 to $87.86 a barrel last night — a 2.45% jump — as traders priced in the risk that the Iran conflict could disrupt oil supply from the Middle East, which produces a large share of the world's crude. Iran sits next to the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20% of global oil passes. Higher oil means higher petrol prices and higher costs for shipping and manufacturing worldwide — it's effectively a tax on the global economy.

stories.title: Airlines Ground Flights Across Middle East as Conflict Resumes
stories.why_it_matters: Multiple airlines have suspended or restricted flights over affected parts of the Middle East following the renewed US-Iran military exchanges. Airlines still operating are being tracked closely. This disrupts international travel and freight routes, adding cost and uncertainty to global supply chains. If you have travel plans through the Middle East, it's worth checking your airline's status.

stories.title: Trump Targets James Comey and Others in Ongoing Political Purge
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration has published a list of individuals it is targeting, including former FBI Director James Comey. The list reportedly includes a range of former officials and public figures seen as political opponents of the administration. This is part of a broader pattern of using government powers against perceived enemies — a democratic norms issue that's drawing international concern about the rule of law in the US, which is still the world's largest economy and a key ally.

stories.title: Trump Administration Moves to Block Mail-In Voting Rule in Appeals Court
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration is asking a federal appeals court to lift a court order that was blocking a new rule restricting mail-in voting. Mail-in voting was widely used during COVID and tends to benefit lower-income and elderly voters who find it harder to vote in person. This legal fight is part of a broader effort to reshape how Americans vote ahead of future elections — the outcome could significantly affect who can participate in US democracy.

markets.summary: A soft night on Wall Street last night — the NASDAQ and S&P 500 both fell, dragged by tech stocks. The ASX closed nearly flat today. Oil is the big mover, spiking on US-Iran tensions. Gold eased slightly and the Aussie dollar dipped a touch.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Effectively flat today — a mild dip of just 9.3 points. The local market shrugged off Wall Street's weakness from last night.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Fell 0.58% last night, weighed by tech sector weakness. Not a dramatic sell-off but a fourth day of caution as Middle East tensions build.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Down 0.64% last night, with big tech names like Google and Microsoft dragging the index lower.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: The standout mover — oil jumped 2.45% on renewed US-Iran military strikes. Watch this closely if it keeps climbing.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold eased slightly despite the geopolitical tension — unusual, as gold often rises as a safe haven. May reflect some profit-taking after a strong run.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar slipped a fraction to 71.5 US cents. Hawkish signals from both the RBA and US Fed are keeping the AUD fairly supported overall.

politics.summary: The big domestic story is building pressure on the RBA to raise interest rates, with analysts warning Australians haven't changed their spending habits enough to bring inflation under control. There's also a new push on telehealth access for voluntary assisted dying.

stories.title: Rate Hike Warning: Aussies Aren't Listening to the RBA
stories.why_it_matters: Analysts are warning the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) may need to lift interest rates again because Australians simply haven't cut their spending enough to bring inflation down to target. The RBA has been trying to slow the economy by making borrowing more expensive, but if consumer spending stays strong, the RBA's hand may be forced. For anyone with a variable-rate mortgage, this is a real concern — another rate rise would push repayments higher again.

stories.title: RBA's Inflation View Out of Touch With Lived Experience, Critics Say
stories.why_it_matters: A commentary piece argues the RBA's inflation data doesn't match what Australians are actually experiencing day-to-day — things like rent, groceries and insurance are hammering household budgets in ways that official statistics understate. This debate matters because it shapes how aggressively the RBA acts on rates. If the RBA is working from data that understates real-world pain, it risks either under- or over-shooting on rate settings, both of which hurt households.

stories.title: Australian Dollar Holds Firm as RBA and Fed Both Seen as Hawkish
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian dollar is holding steady around 71.5 US cents because currency traders see both the RBA and the US Federal Reserve as likely to keep interest rates higher for longer — 'hawkish' is finance-speak for leaning toward rate increases rather than cuts. A stronger AUD is generally good for Australians travelling or buying imports, but can hurt exporters. For your US shareholdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO), a stronger AUD means their value in Australian dollars is slightly reduced.

stories.title: Push for Telehealth Access to Voluntary Assisted Dying
stories.why_it_matters: There's growing political pressure on the Prime Minister to allow voluntary assisted dying (VAD) consultations to happen via telehealth — currently, patients often need to physically travel to access these services, which is a major barrier for people in rural areas or who are too ill to travel. Advocates argue telehealth access is a basic equity issue. The PM has not yet committed to a change, making this an ongoing political pressure point on the government's health policy agenda.

ai.summary: The big AI story today is geopolitical: the US is pushing G20 nations to take a 'hands-off' approach to regulating AI. Meanwhile, there's a battle brewing between big banks and big tech over how AI 'agents' (AI that can take actions on your behalf) should be regulated, and the global financial watchdog is sounding alarms.

stories.title: US Pushes G20 to Keep Hands Off AI Regulation
stories.why_it_matters: The US is formally pushing G20 nations (the world's 20 biggest economies, including Australia) to adopt what it's calling the 'Carolina Principles' — a framework for keeping AI regulation light and innovation-friendly rather than imposing strict rules. This is a direct counter to the European Union's approach of heavy AI regulation. The outcome matters enormously: if the world's major economies agree to keep AI relatively unregulated, that's a green light for tech companies to develop and deploy AI faster — good for stocks like GOOG, MSFT and GXAI.

stories.title: Banks vs Big Tech: The Fight Over 'Agentic AI' Rules
stories.why_it_matters: A new regulatory battle is forming in Australia and globally between big banks and big tech companies over how to handle 'agentic AI' — that's AI systems that don't just answer questions but actually take actions on your behalf, like booking a flight or moving your money. Banks want strict rules because AI agents could cause financial harm if they go wrong; tech companies want freedom to innovate. The outcome will shape how AI assistants are allowed to work in banking and finance — directly affecting how you might interact with your bank in the near future.

stories.title: Global Financial Watchdog Warns on 'Frontier AI' Risks
stories.why_it_matters: The Financial Stability Board — the international body that monitors risks to the global financial system — has issued a formal warning about 'frontier AI models', meaning the most advanced and powerful AI systems being developed right now. They're worried these systems could introduce new risks to financial stability that regulators aren't equipped to handle yet. This is the global financial system's equivalent of a yellow warning flag — not a ban, but a signal that scrutiny is coming.

stories.title: Broadcom Launches 'VMware AI Factory' for Enterprise AI Agents
stories.why_it_matters: Broadcom has launched a new product called the 'VMware AI Factory' — essentially a secure, managed platform that lets large companies (banks, hospitals, manufacturers) run AI agents safely within their own systems. Think of it as a controlled environment where AI can do useful work without the security risks of connecting to the open internet. This is the kind of enterprise AI infrastructure buildout that is driving massive spending across the tech sector — and is a key reason why companies like Microsoft and Google are investing so heavily in AI data centres.

sport.summary: NRL Round 27 is almost here with the draw kicking off Thursday night. The Sharks are pushing for home finals, there's a contentious kick-off rule change being trialled again, and Jarome Luai has touched down in PNG for his new club. In AFL, Geelong is apparently making a massive play for Fremantle's Josh Caddy-era star Bobby Hill... wait, it's actually Patrick Butters drawing eye-watering interest.

stories.title: Sharks Fight for Home Finals at Their Own Ground
stories.why_it_matters: The Cronulla Sharks are lobbying the NRL to play their home finals match at their actual home ground — Ocean Protect Stadium — rather than being shifted to a larger neutral venue. With finals just around the corner, this is a significant stadium politics battle. The Sharks feel their fans deserve a home finals atmosphere at their own ground, and the NRL's decision will set a precedent for other clubs in similar situations.

stories.title: NRL's Kick-Off Rule Change to Be Trialled Again
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL's contentious kick-off rule change — which drew significant backlash when previously trialled — is set to be tested again. The rule changes how kick-offs are taken and has divided coaches and fans. Trialling it again suggests the NRL is seriously considering making it permanent, which would alter game flow and strategy across the competition.

stories.title: Jarome Luai Arrives in PNG for NRL Chiefs Debut
stories.why_it_matters: Former Panthers and Eels halfback Jarome Luai has landed in Papua New Guinea as the first big-name signing for the NRL's new PNG franchise — a historic moment for rugby league in the Pacific. His arrival signals the new club is serious about competing, and there's already debate about whether Parramatta will regret letting him go. Luai was a premiership winner with Penrith and was a marquee capture for the PNG expansion team.

stories.title: Geelong Make Eye-Watering Offer for Fremantle's Patrick Butters
stories.why_it_matters: Geelong are reportedly putting an 'eye-watering' contract offer to Fremantle Docker Patrick Butters in what would be one of the AFL trade period's biggest moves. Butters is a highly-rated midfielder, and if Geelong can prise him away from Fremantle it would be a major statement of intent from the Cats. The Herald Sun reports the offer is substantial — details of the dollar figure haven't been confirmed, but sources describe it as a number designed to be very hard to knock back.
